# Where Do Sample Size Inputs Come From? {#sec-input-sources}

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple" title="Learning objectives"}
- Find defensible planning estimates.
- Explain uncertainty in pilot and historical values.
:::

## The idea

Anticipated prevalence, event risks, mean differences, standard deviations, ICC and AUC should be linked to relevant populations, instruments, outcomes and follow-up intervals. Candidate sources include systematic reviews, high-quality comparable studies, registries, feasibility studies and preliminary pilot work. Every borrowed estimate needs an explicit citation and rationale for transportability.

## When and how to apply it

Do not confuse a statistically significant result in an earlier paper with a clinically important target difference. When plausible inputs vary, calculate a sensitivity range rather than relying on one overly precise assumption. Record the outcome definition, denominators, follow-up time and study setting for each source.

## Teaching case 1 — baseline draft

::: {.callout-tip appearance="simple" title="Clinical scenario / initial worked example"}
A prior study reports diabetes distress prevalence of 33% in a tertiary clinic. Would that be a defensible input for an urban primary-care sample? Document what must be checked.
:::

::: {.callout-warning appearance="simple" title="Common error"}
A small pilot SD is uncertain; using it as if known exactly can understate the risk of inadequate power.
:::

Every planning parameter needs a plausible source and sensitivity range.
